responses.response: Use an element-creation step first, because rich descriptions are a follow-up step after the element exists. For the processing service, create the service or container first, then use a normal system-model description: short prose by default, with a sparse metadata block only if you truly need queryable fields such as owner or regions. For the production VM, create the deployment node first, then use a markdown table inside the description as the primary format, with network interfaces first; add deployment metadata only if automation will query IP, OS, RTO, or similar fields.

For ProdApiVm, use one markdown table in the description. Put information in this order: network interfaces first, then OS, then hardware such as CPU, RAM, and Disk, then service or runtime details that help operators, then operational properties such as RTO, RPO, or monitoring cadence. Include only rows that are actually useful to operators. Do not duplicate the hostname because that is already the VM title, the gateway because that belongs on the zone, firewall rules or monitoring links because they are shown by relationships or the diagram, service endpoints because they belong to relationships and instanceOf, or tags because they should stay in #tags. Add a metadata block only if the same fields must be queried by automation.

Keep it to a single table and make it scan-friendly. Put eth0 and eth1 first, then OS, then hardware such as CPU, RAM, GPU, and Disk if they matter for capacity or troubleshooting, then only the operational rows that drive action on call, such as runtime, health check, RTO, and maybe RPO. Do not dump every implementation detail into the block; if a value does not help an operator diagnose, route, recover, or automate, leave it out. Also do not repeat hostname, gateway, relationships, or tags. If automation needs the same data for inventory, compliance, or capacity planning, duplicate only those key fields into metadata; otherwise skip metadata entirely.
